title: Act IV, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At Fife, Lady Macduff tells Ross that her husband's flight was madness and that he loves them not; Ross defends him as wise and leaves. She tells her son his father is dead and a traitor; the clever boy banters that the liars and swearers are enough to beat the honest men and hang them up. A messenger warns her to flee. Murderers enter, call Macduff a traitor, and stab the boy ('He has kill'd me, mother'); she runs out crying 'Murder!' and is pursued.

context.history: The scene is one of very few in Shakespeare to show a child killed on stage. It is the moment many audiences turn wholly against Macbeth.

significance: The domestic warmth and wit of mother and son make the violence unbearable and show Macbeth's tyranny reaching the defenseless. It also raises the question of why Macduff left his family.
discussionQuestions: Is it ever right to leave your family to fight for a larger cause?
Where does irony appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with masculinity, power and violence?

satQuestions.passage:
What had he done, to make him fly the land?
You must have patience, madam.
He had none:
His flight was madness: when our actions do not,
Our fears do make us traitors.
You know not
Whether it was his wisdom or his fear.
Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes,
His mansion and his titles in a place
From whence himself does fly? He loves us not;
He wants the natural touch: for the poor wren,
The most diminutive of birds, will fight,
Her young ones in her nest, against the owl.
All is the fear and nothing is the love;
As little is the wisdom, where the flight
So runs against all reason.

anchorPassages.text:
Was my father a traitor, mother?
Ay, that he was.
What is a traitor?
Why, one that swears and lies.
And be all traitors that do so?
Every one that does so is a traitor, and must be hanged.
And must they all be hanged that swear and lie?
Every one.
Who must hang them?
Why, the honest men.
Then the liars and swearers are fools, for there are liars and swearers enow to beat the honest men and hang up them.
Now, God help thee, poor monkey!
But how wilt thou do for a father?
If he were dead, you’d weep for him: if you would not, it were a good sign that I should quickly have a new father.
Poor prattler, how thou talk’st!
Enter a Messenger.
Bless you, fair dame! I am not to you known,
Though in your state of honour I am perfect.
I doubt some danger does approach you nearly:
If you will take a homely man’s advice,
Be not found here; hence, with your little ones.
To fright you thus, methinks, I am too savage;
To do worse to you were fell cruelty,
Which is too nigh your person. Heaven preserve you!
I dare abide no longer.

I am in this earthly world; where to do harm
Is often laudable, to do good sometime
Accounted dangerous folly: why then, alas,
Do I put up that womanly defence,
To say I have done no harm?
Then the liars and swearers are fools, for there are liars and swearers enow to beat the honest men and hang up them.

wordHistories: “laudable”: Origin: Old French laudable; earlier Latin laudabilis.
“swearers”: Origin of “swearer”: an English formation from swear + -er.

segments.script: The scene is one of very few in Shakespeare to show a child killed on stage. It is the moment many audiences turn wholly against Macbeth. The domestic warmth and wit of mother and son make the violence unbearable and show Macbeth's tyranny reaching the defenseless. It also raises the question of why Macduff left his family. Characterization: Lady Macduff and her son talk about traitors; the son is witty and brave. Dramatic irony: A messenger warns them too late; murderers arrive. Structure: The only domestic scene in the play: innocence slaughtered. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “He loves us not; / He wants the natural touch” slowly and put it in my own words: Lady Macduff tells Ross that Macduff does not love his family, since he fled and left them unprotected. Next, craft. I notice the bitter comparison she goes on to make with a small bird that fights to protect its nest. The strongest word is “natural”: it means the instinctive love that makes even animals defend their young. Then, effect. Why does Lady Macduff say her husband lacks "the natural touch"? My answer: Lady Macduff says her husband lacks "the natural touch" because he fled and left his family unprotected, unlike even a small bird; she does not know he went to raise an army, which makes the coming murder more painful.
